Bumble on Tuesday said it would now allow either person in a match to send the first message, dropping the women-first messaging rule that has been ⁠a defining feature of the dating app since its launch in 2014.

The move comes as dating-app companies grapple with user fatigue toward traditional swipe-based platforms and slowing growth, prompting some ⁠including Bumble and Tinder-owner Match ⁠Group to roll out new features and AI-powered tools aimed at improving engagement.

Thus far, only women could initiate conversations in heterosexual matches on Bumble, unlike most dating apps, including Tinder, where either user can send the first message.

Bumble said tests in Canada have shown higher chat initiation rates, fewer ⁠expired chats and more mutual conversations after the changes were introduced.

The company is also extending the reply window to 72 hours from 24 hours as it looks to increase conversations and reduce the number of matches that expire without interaction.

The changes are a response to demands from users for “more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to ⁠create real, meaningful connections,” founder and CEO ⁠Whitney Wolfe Herd said.

headline: Stock market today: BSE Sensex, NSE Nifty50 expected to open in red
body: Indian stock markets are entering a period where global developments could have a bigger influence on trading sentiment. Crude oil prices remain an i
full_body:
Indian equity markets are expected to open on a mildly negative note, with Gift Nifty trading around 24,603, down 28 points, indicating a subdued start for domestic indices. Global cues remain mixed as investors balance easing US rate concerns against elevated crude oil prices and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty around the Middle East. With U.S. July CPI data due this week, markets are likely to remain cautious and sensitive to inflation and interest-rate expectations.

Asian equities traded with a cautious bias as investors assessed the latest developments in the Middle East and their impact on oil prices and inflation. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan moved between gains and losses before edging 0.2% higher, while South Korea’s Kospi rose 0.3%. The mixed trend came after hopes of a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz weakened, sending US crude prices up about 5% in the previous session.

Higher oil prices are a concern for Asian economies that rely heavily on energy imports, as they can add to inflation and put pressure on economic growth. US stock futures offered some support, with Nasdaq futures up 0.28% and S&P 500 futures 0.1% higher. European futures were subdued, with EUROSTOXX 50 down 0.05%, while FTSE and DAX futures were flat. Investors were also awaiting US inflation data for clues on the Federal Reserve’s rate path.

Crude oil prices remained close to their highest levels in more than a week as hopes of a quick agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz weakened. WTI crude was around $82.22 a barrel, while Brent crude was near $87.80, after both benchmarks had gained more than 5% in the previous session.

The strategic waterway is particularly important for global energy markets because it handles a significant share of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Any prolonged disruption could keep energy prices elevated and raise concerns about inflation, transport costs and corporate margins.

Analysts have highlighted a combination of geopolitical uncertainty, crude oil prices and upcoming economic data as key factors likely to influence Indian equities. Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, founder and CEO of HST Wealth, said markets remained in a wait-and-watch mode as uncertainty over a lasting Middle East settlement and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz limited aggressive risk-taking.

Vinod Nair, head of research at Geojit Investments, also pointed to the tension around the strategic waterway, while noting that corporate earnings were providing some support to broader sentiment.

Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, said that rising crude prices and Middle East uncertainty had offset optimism from weaker-than-expected US jobs data.

Ever been stuck doom scrolling Swiggy because you cannot decide what to eat? Thanks to food delivery apps, we are spoilt for choice — a little too much one might say. Start-up founder Akshay Bhartiya is solving this problem with his new app called Luckd. With this food delivery app, you do not have to select the dishes you want. They deliver surprise mystery bags from popular cafes and restaurants in the city. Here is how it works.

“When I lived in the UK, we had fewer options for delivery, but it was more curated. In India we are bombarded with too many options . What we are building is a marketplace for curated experiences. headline: Teaching AI to speak India
body: Artificial intelligence can chat, translate and answer questions but only if it understands your language. At IIT Madras, researchers at AI4Bharat are travelling across India, collecting voices, preserving dialects and teaching AI to understand the country’s incredible linguistic diversity.

“Nani, aaj kya banaya?” (”Grandma, what did you cook today?”)

It’s a simple question that millions of Indians ask every day. But what if you asked it to an AI assistant? Would it understand the language? The accent? The mix of Hindi and English? What if the question was asked in Tulu, Bundeli, Kodava or Santali instead?

Artificial intelligence has become more advanced at answering questions, translating languages and even writing stories. But there’s a catch. Most AI systems learnt these skills from enormous amounts of digital data — books, websites, videos and conversations, much of it in English. For many Indian languages and dialects, especially those spoken by smaller communities, that kind of digital treasure trove simply doesn’t exist.

So how do you teach a machine to understand a country where languages change every few hundred kilometres, accents shift from district to district, and some words are spoken every day but have never been written down?

That’s the challenge researchers at AI4Bharat, a research lab at IIT Madras, have taken on. Their mission is ambitious: to build AI that can understand, speak and translate India’s many languages, making technology more accessible to millions. We spoke to Kaushal Bhogale, a PhD researcher at AI4Bharat, to find out how his team is teaching AI to speak India, one voice, one conversation and one language at a time.

When people think of artificial intelligence, they often assume it can understand every language equally well. In reality, AI is only as good as the information it learns from.

headline: Why is it called the shift key?
body: Technology keeps shifting. In this case, shift kept shifting quite literally. Confused? Here’s how your favourite shift key got it’s name
full_body:
Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription

Today's Cache Your download of the top 5 technology stories of the day.

Have you ever looked at a keyboard and wondered why there is a key called ‘shift’ staring at you? That too, not just on one side, but one on each side, with an upward arrow next to it. Sometimes the key becomes just the upward arrow as well, like how it is shown on phone keyboards.

What is this key? Why is it called the ‘shift’ key? Read on to know more about its origin story!

Fun fact: the shift key was never an invention made for computers. It began way back in the late 1800s when typewriters were the star of the show.

A journey which lasted years and years, typewriters have evolved over time. From not having a keyboard structure to forming the QWERTY layout we see today to the shift and caps lock keys we see today — typewriters and keyboards have come a long way.

It was around 1878 that the idea of the shift key was executed on a typewriter — the Remington No. 2 typewriter — created by the E. Remington and Sons company. Typewriters till then either only had one set of capital letters to type anything out or were bulky with two sets of ‘keyboards’ (one lowercase and the other uppercase), which had to be used alternatively whenever needed. The initial Remington typewriter also did not have the shift key.

In 1878, the Remington No. 2 Typewriter adopted the first shift key instead of adding a second keyboard — basically one keyboard and a mechanical shift to access uppercase letters and extra symbols. This enabled the typers to easily shift between lowercase, uppercase and even symbols.

The launch of the feature and its quick rollback showed how easily even casual internet users broke past Google’s enterprise-level safeguards in order to create deepfake satellite images, in spite of the risks they pose.

Put simply, users could open Google Earth—the company’s immersive satellite map of the planet—in order to zoom into a place, choose the “create image” option, and type whatever they wanted to see built on top of the original imagery.

On July 30, Google Earth’s Product Manager Bryan Horowitz shared a blog post that invited users to “transform any place,” with AI, the process powered by the company’s image generation Nano Banana technology.

Google suggested several wholesome use cases for the feature, such as re-imagining (not visualising) how modern-day landmarks looked in ancient times, as well as generating mock-ups of completed real estate projects, creating educational infographics, and giving real-life locations a fantasy feel. Teachers, architects, and urban planners were invited to get creative with the prompts, and Google shared examples as well.

On July 31, the company posted an update to its launch blog post, confirming that the AI feature in Google Earth had been rolled back over possible policy violations by others.

“We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world. We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies. So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails,” stated the update, adding, “It’s important to note that generated images didn’t appear in the main Google Earth experience for others to see and were watermarked as AI generated.”
